questions.knowledge_point: Finding the General Solution of a Differential Equation Using Integration
questions.problem: Find the general solution to the differential equation  ${f}^{′}(x)=\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡4x.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, notice that the derivative term is already isolated on the left:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡4x.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate both sides of the equation with respect to $x,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {f}^{′}(x)\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡4x\,\text{d}x \\ f(x) & =\frac{1}{2}\int \operatorname{sin}⁡4x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(-\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{cos}⁡4x) \\  & =-\frac{1}{8}\operatorname{cos}⁡4x+C.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Find the general solution to the differential equation  ${f}^{′}(x)+3{e}^{-x}=0.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we rearrange the equation to isolate the derivative term:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =-3{e}^{-x}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate both sides of the equation with respect to $x,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {f}^{′}(x)\,\text{d}x & =\int (-3{e}^{-x})\text{d}x \\ f(x) & =-3\int {e}^{-x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =-3(-{e}^{-x})+C \\  & =3{e}^{-x}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Solve the differential equation $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+4{e}^{2x}=-2x.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we rearrange the equation to isolate the derivative term:

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=-4{e}^{2x}-2x.
$$

Then, we integrate both sides of the equation with respect to $x,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =\int (-4{e}^{2x}-2x)\,\text{d}x \\ y & =\int (-4{e}^{2x}-2x)\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}y & =\int (-4{e}^{2x}-2x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =-4\int {e}^{2x}\,\text{d}x-2\int x\,\text{d}x \\  & =-2{e}^{2x}-{x}^{2}+C.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Find the general solution to the differential equation  ${f}^{′}(x)+6{x}^{2}=4x.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we rearrange the equation to isolate the derivative term:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =4x-6{x}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate both sides of the equation with respect to $x,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {f}^{′}(x)\,\text{d}x & =\int (4x-6{x}^{2})\text{d}x \\  & =4\int x\,\text{d}x-6\int {x}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =4\cdot \frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}-6\cdot \frac{1}{3}{x}^{3} \\  & =2{x}^{2}-2{x}^{3}+C \\  & =2{x}^{2}(1-x)+C.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.worked_solution:
First, we rearrange the equation to isolate the derivative term:

$$

Then, we integrate both sides of the equation with respect to $x,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {f}^{′}(x)\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{3}{5}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)\,\text{d}x \\ f(x) & =\int \frac{3}{5}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the General Solution of a Second Order Differential Equation by Integrating Twice
questions.problem: Solve the differential equation $\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}=20{x}^{3}.$
questions.worked_solution:
Integrating the equation once, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & =20\int {x}^{3}\,\text{d}x \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =20\cdot \frac{1}{4}{x}^{4}+C \\  & =5{x}^{4}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Integrating a second time, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =\int (5{x}^{4}+C)\text{d}x \\ y & =5\cdot \frac{1}{5}{x}^{5}+Cx+D \\  & ={x}^{5}+Cx+D.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that because we had a second-order equation, our general solution contains *two* arbitrary constants, $C$ and $D.$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the General Solution of a Second Order Differential Equation by Integrating Twice
questions.problem:
Solve the differential equation

$$
\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}+5=6{x}^{2}.
$$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we rearrange the equation to give

$$
\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}=6{x}^{2}-5.
$$

Now, integrating the equation once, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & =\int (6{x}^{2}-5)\text{d}x \\  & =6\int {x}^{2}\,\text{d}x-5\int \text{d}x \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =6(\frac{{x}^{3}}{3})-5x+C \\  & =2{x}^{3}-5x+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Integrating a second time, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =\int (2{x}^{3}-5x+C)\text{d}x \\ y & =2\int {x}^{3}\,\text{d}x-5\int x\,\text{d}x+C\int \text{d}x \\  & =2(\frac{{x}^{4}}{4})-5(\frac{{x}^{2}}{2})+Cx+D \\  & =\frac{{x}^{4}}{2}-\frac{5{x}^{2}}{2}+Cx+D.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that because we had a second-order equation, our general solution contains *two* arbitrary constants, $C$ and $D.$

questions.problem: Solve the differential equation $2\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}-\operatorname{sin}⁡x=4x.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we rearrange the equation to give

$$
\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}=2x+\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡x.
$$

Now, integrating the equation once, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & =\int (2x+\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡x)\text{d}x \\  & =2\int x\,\text{d}x+\frac{1}{2}\int \operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =2(\frac{{x}^{2}}{2})+\frac{1}{2}(-\operatorname{cos}⁡x)+C \\  & ={x}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡x+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Integrating a second time, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =\int ({x}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡x+C)\,\text{d}x \\ y & =\int {x}^{2}\,\text{d}x-\frac{1}{2}\int \operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x+C\int \text{d}x \\  & =(\frac{{x}^{3}}{3})-\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{sin}⁡x)+Cx+D \\  & =\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡x+Cx+D.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that because we had a second-order equation, our general solution contains *two* arbitrary constants, $C$ and $D.$

$$

First, we rearrange the equation to give

$$
\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}=8{e}^{x/2}-6x.
$$

Now, integrating the equation once, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & =\int (8{e}^{x/2}-6x)\text{d}x \\  & =8\int {e}^{x/2}\,\text{d}x-6\int x\,\text{d}x \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =8(2{e}^{x/2})-6(\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2})+C \\  & =16{e}^{x/2}-3{x}^{2}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Integrating a second time, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =\int (16{e}^{x/2}-3{x}^{2}+C)\text{d}x \\ y & =16\int {e}^{x/2}\,\text{d}x-3\int {x}^{2}\,\text{d}x+C\int \text{d}x \\  & =16(2{e}^{x/2})-3(\frac{1}{3}{x}^{3})+Cx+D \\  & =32{e}^{x/2}-{x}^{3}+Cx+D.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that because we had a second-order equation, our general solution contains *two* arbitrary constants, $C$ and $D.$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Solution of a Differential Equation With a Given Condition
questions.problem: Find the particular solution to the differential equation ${f}^{′}(x)+2\operatorname{cos}⁡x=0$ that satisfies the condition $f(0)=-1.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we rearrange the equation to give

$$
{f}^{′}(x)=-2\operatorname{cos}⁡x.
$$

Then, we integrate both sides with respect to $x,$ and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {f}^{′}(x)\,\text{d}x & =\int (-2\operatorname{cos}⁡x)\,\text{d}x \\ f(x) & =-2\int \operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =-2\operatorname{sin}⁡x+C.\end{aligned}
$$

So our general solution is $y=-2\operatorname{sin}⁡x+C.$ To find a particular solution, we substitute the condition $f(0)=-1$ into our solution and obtain a value for $C,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}-1 & =-2\operatorname{sin}⁡0+C \\ -1 & =-2(0)+C \\ C & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our particular solution is

$$
f(x)=-2\operatorname{sin}⁡x-1.
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Solution of a Differential Equation With a Given Condition
questions.problem: Find the particular solution to the differential equation ${y}^{′}+{e}^{-2x}=8x$ that satisfies the condition $y(0)=1.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we rearrange the equation to give

$$
{y}^{′}=8x-{e}^{-2x}.
$$

Then, we integrate both sides with respect to $x,$ and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {y}^{′}\,\text{d}x & =\int (8x-{e}^{-2x})\,\text{d}x \\ y & =8\int x\,\text{d}x-\int {e}^{-2x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =8(\frac{{x}^{2}}{2})-(-\frac{{e}^{-2x}}{2})+C \\  & =4{x}^{2}+\frac{{e}^{-2x}}{2}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

So our general solution is $y=4{x}^{2}+\frac{{e}^{-2x}}{2}+C.$ To find a particular solution, we substitute the condition $y(0)=1$ into our solution and obtain a value for $C,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}1 & =4(0)^{2}+\frac{{e}^{-2(0)}}{2}+C \\ 1 & =0+\frac{1}{2}+C \\ C & =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our particular solution is

$$
y=4{x}^{2}+\frac{{e}^{-2x}}{2}+\frac{1}{2}.
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {y}^{′}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{8}{(x-3)^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\ y & =8\int \frac{1}{(x-3)^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =8(-\frac{1}{x-3})+C \\  & =-\frac{8}{x-3}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$
y=-\frac{8}{x-3}+9.

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Solution of a Differential Equation With a Given Condition
questions.problem:
Find the particular solution to the differential equation below that satisfies the condition $f(0)=-2.$

$$
(1+2x){f}^{′}(x)-2=0.
$$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we rearrange the equation to give

$$
{f}^{′}(x)=\frac{2}{1+2x}.
$$

Then, we integrate both sides with respect to $x,$ and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {f}^{′}(x)\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{2}{1+2x}\,\text{d}x \\ f(x) & =\int \frac{2}{1+2x}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Let $u=(1+2x).$ Then $\text{d}u=2\,\text{d}x.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\int \frac{2}{1+2x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{1}{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡|u|+C \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡|1+2x|+C.\end{aligned}
$$

So our general solution is $f(x)=\operatorname{ln}⁡|1+2x|+C.$ To find a particular solution, we substitute the condition $f(0)=-2$ into our solution and obtain a value for $C,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡|1+2x|+C \\ -2 & =\operatorname{ln}⁡|1+2\cdot 0|+C \\ -2 & =\operatorname{ln}⁡|1|+C \\ C & =-2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our particular solution is

$$
f(x)=\operatorname{ln}⁡|1+2x|-2.
$$

Then, we integrate both sides with respect to $x,$ and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {f}^{′}(x)\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{3}{1+{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\ f(x) & =3\int \frac{1}{1+{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =3\operatorname{arctan}⁡x+C.\end{aligned}
$$

So our general solution is $f(x) = 3\arctan{x} + C.$ To find a particular solution, we substitute the condition $f(0) = 2$ into our solution and obtain a value for $C,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =3\operatorname{arctan}⁡(x)+C \\ 2 & =3\operatorname{arctan}⁡(0)+C \\ 2 & =0+C \\ C & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our particular solution is 

$$
f(x)=3\arctan x + 2.
$$
